summary.text: The bathypelagic or midnight zone is the open-ocean layer from 1,000 to 4,000 m deep, lying between the mesopelagic above and the abyssopelagic below.
With no sunlight for photosynthesis, its life is fed mainly by organic matter sinking from the waters above, sometimes called marine snow.
It keeps a nearly constant temperature of about 4 °C, and its water pressure ranges from 100 to 400 atmospheres.

facts.label: Lysocline depth
facts.value: About 3,500 m, near the zone's base

items.prompt: A biologist tows a net at 2,000 m in the open ocean. Why will she find no phytoplankton growing there?

options.label: The water there is far too salty
No sunlight reaches for photosynthesis
Fish there eat every last one
The water there is too warm

items.explain: Sunlight does not reach this deep, so photosynthesis-driven production and phytoplankton growth cannot happen.

items.prompt: A fish living at 3,000 m never sees daylight. Where does most of the food in its world come from?

options.label: Chemicals pouring out of hydrothermal vents
Plants rooted on the dark seafloor
Particles of dead matter sinking from above
Minerals dissolved out of seabed rock

items.explain: Sinking organic matter such as fecal pellets and dead organisms is the main way food reaches this zone; chemoautotrophy plays a more minor role.

items.prompt: Pressure grows by about 1 atmosphere for every 10 m of depth. A submersible sinks from 1,000 m to 2,000 m. Roughly how much does the pressure on it rise?

options.label: About 10 atmospheres
About 1,000 atmospheres
About 1 atmosphere
About 100 atmospheres

items.explain: At 1 atmosphere per 10 m, an extra 1,000 m adds about 100 atmospheres, which is why pressure here spans 100 to 400 atmospheres.

items.prompt: Equal amounts of dead surface matter sink as tiny scattered specks or as larger clumps. Which is more likely to reach 3,000 m?

options.label: The clumps, which fall faster and get eaten less
The specks, which slip past hungry animals
Neither, since nothing sinks that far down
Both equally, since size does not matter

items.explain: Small particles that clump together sink faster and escape being eaten, so they are more likely to reach great depths.

items.prompt: Microbes crowd around a hydrothermal vent in the pitch-dark bathypelagic. What do they use as their energy source?

options.label: Faint sunlight filtering down from above
Light given off by glowing animals
Oxygen bubbling out of the vent
Chemicals such as sulfide and methane

items.explain: Vents deliver chemicals like sulfide and methane, which organisms use for energy through chemoautotrophy instead of sunlight.

items.prompt: Calcite shells of tiny sea creatures sink into ever deeper, colder, higher-pressure water. What tends to happen to them?

options.label: They harden and grow thicker
They dissolve more readily
They float back toward the surface
They stay exactly as they were

items.explain: As depth and pressure rise and temperature falls, calcium carbonate becomes more soluble, so more of it dissolves.
